Anyone who undertakes to enter upon any discipline must know its foundational principles, its definition, and the definition of this science. The definition of this science is the knowledge by which the meanings of the speech of Allah are understood, and its name is the science of tafsīr (exegesis). Tafsīr and taʾwīl are not one and the same in meaning. Tafsīr means the explanation of the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, from the perspective of what has been transmitted. Taʾwīl means [explanation] through the exercise of reason (al-ʿaql). Both tafsīr and taʾwīl must rest upon transmission or reason, [and the Prophet] ﷺ forbade the interpretation of the Qur'ān based upon personal opinion (al-raʾy). No one should interpret the Qur'ān by his own desire without [knowledge] transmitted to him.
When ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face, was asked: "Do you possess a book that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ singled out for the People of the House?" He replied: "No,

except the Book of Allah, or an understanding that Allah has granted to a Muslim man."[1] And ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face, said: "The Qur'ān is pliable—possessing multiple faces—so accept its faces."[2] Whoever clings to something [derived] from the Qur'ān has a basis for his claim. [The Qur'ān] can be exercised through reason in order to understand the meanings of the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. It has been narrated from the Prophet ﷺ that he forbade the interpretation of the Qur'ān based upon personal opinion.[3] Necessarily, the interpretation of the Qur'ān requires knowledge of the Arabic language, knowledge of legal ordinances (al-aḥkām al-sharʿiyya), knowledge of rhetoric (al-bayān) and the art of eloquent expression (al-badīʿ), and necessarily there must be a light in the heart of the mufassir (exegete).[4]

Knowledge of the Arabic language, knowledge of legal ordinances (sharīʿa), knowledge of rhetoric (bayān) and eloquent expression (badīʿ), and necessarily there must be a light in the heart of the exegete.[4]

This Book, Allah has sent down to us as guidance and as light. It is not like other composed books—not a dry, worldly legal code, not a medical treatise by which diseases and remedies are understood, not a history recording events and occurrences, not a book of artistic rhetoric intended for musical pleasure. For all these arts are within the power of human understanding to compose their like. Yet this Book came as guidance and light, transcending all of these and encompassing all of these—a constitution both worldly and otherworldly from the time of its revelation to the end of time. Every code that governs human affairs is covered therein. Every aspect of human life—birth, childhood, adolescence, adulthood, and old age—has been encompassed by the guidance of this Book.

This Book, which came as guidance and light, transcends all worldly standards and encompasses all of them—a constitution both worldly and otherworldly from the time of its revelation unto the end of ages. Every standard that covers [the governance of] human affairs is included within it. Every age has need of guidance from the Qur'ān. Just as in the age of the Prophet ﷺ the Qur'ān was the guidance by which he established justice and equity among people, so too in every age thereafter, when the community returns to the Qur'ān, it will find therein what suffices it for its circumstances and conditions.

[Allah, the Exalted, says:] "And We shall strengthen them with a spirit from Us, [and those who have disbelieved after it—those are the ones [in loss]."[5] God has promised: "He will surely establish for them their religion which He has chosen for them, and will surely replace, after the fear they [now] experience, with security and peace" (Q. 24:55). They worship Allah, not associating anything with Him—this is the true pillar upon which worship is built. Not the multiplication of actions, nor the perfection of form, but rather sincerity and the absence of association. For Allah says: "And We send not the messengers except as bringers of good tidings and warners" (Q. 25:56), and again: "Say: 'I do not ask of you for it any reward except love for my near relatives'" (Q. 42:23). This promise [of Allah] was realized for us, confirmed by Allah, so that our hope was strengthened that everything Allah has promised us in the Qur'ān we shall find exactly as He has promised.

When the community became heedless of this Book, there were set over them the Europeans and Yaʾjūj wa-Maʾjūj of the East, and they overpowered them, so that they lost the mighty dignity (ʿizz) which they had acquired through the Qur'ān. Yet the promise remains: "He will surely establish for them their religion which He has chosen for them." This promise is not abrogated. When the community returns to this Qur'ān—to its understanding, its application, and its principles—they will restore what they have lost.

The Qur'ān was revealed with a promise at the beginning of its revelation. Allah, Exalted, has fulfilled that promise for us with a fulfillment that strengthens our hope in everything that Allah has promised us in this [Book]. The sessions of tafsīr (exegetical study), from the time of the Prophet ﷺ until our day, have been continuously supported and expanded by Allah, Blessed and Exalted. The diversity of tafāsīr (exegetical works), this Qur'ān was revealed with a promise at its beginning, and Allah, Blessed and Exalted, has fulfilled that promise for us—a fulfillment that fills us with strength of hope in everything that Allah has promised us in the Qur'ān, so that we find it exactly as He has promised.
And the sessions of tafsīr from the time of the Prophet ﷺ until this very day, have had no precedent in all history.[7]

I declare that these three promises have been fulfilled for us by Allah in such wise that our hope has been strengthened: that everything Allah has promised us in the Qur'ān we shall find exactly as He has promised, even as He has promised it, and in the manner that He has promised it. And the sessions of exegesis have continued to be blessed and multiplied, a sign that Allah confirms the promise He made in His Book, and a sign for us that every promise in the Qur'ān shall be fulfilled.

And the interpretation of the Qur'ān is a science that is the noblest of all sciences, for the nobility of any science is measured by the nobility of its object (mutaʿallaquh). And this is the speech of Allah—its relation to our speech is like the relation of truth to creation. The Qur'ān is the word of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and everything contained therein is truth and guidance. Therefore the science devoted to understanding it must be the noblest of sciences.

And the Qur'ān has many names, and the multiplicity of names indicates the nobility of what is named. There are mentioned in the Qur'ān fifty-five names for the Qur'ān itself: it is called the Qur'ān, it is called the Dhikr (Remembrance), it is called the Furqān (Criterion), it is called the Kitāb (Book), it is called the Nūr (Light), it is called the Hudā (Guidance), and other noble names that indicate the nobility of this Book and the nobility of the science devoted to it.

"By the Truth"—and this distinction which returns to the servant after his annihilation (fanāʾ) is perfection, for it grants to each who has a right his right and fulfills for each who has a share his share. So no distinction veils him from seeing Allah, Blessed and Exalted. The heart, too, divests itself of all blameworthy traits and adorns itself with all praiseworthy ones. The spirit abandons attending to anything except Allah, Blessed and Exalted. And the innermost secret (sirr) is annihilated in the Essence of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, beholding nothing else—this is the complete entry into Islam.

["I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed."] The wisdom in beginning the recitation of the Qur'ān with this utterance—that entering into the royal presence requires knocking at the door and requires seeking refuge. One does not enter upon a great king without first seeking permission and asking for protection. So too, one does not begin reading the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, without first seeking refuge in Him from Satan, the accursed, and without asking for His protection and assistance.

"I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Thus Gabriel taught it to me—from the Tablet, from the Pen, from the Lord, Blessed and Exalted." This formula represents the most excellent form of seeking refuge.[8]

"I seek refuge"—I take refuge with Allah, Blessed and Exalted; I cry out for His protection. "In Allah"—in the Almighty, Blessed and Exalted. "From Satan"—from Iblīs himself. Satan (al-shaytān) derives from the root shaṭana (to distance). Iblīs was once a servant held in high honor in the divine presence, as his story will unfold hereafter. Yet he was cast out, cursed, and expelled from the proximity of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, whereupon he was named Satan and called Iblīs—a name he bore after his former name, ʿAzāzīl.[10] The appellation "the accursed" (al-rajīm) denotes one who is stoned, expelled from the divine presence, cast out from Paradise, driven from the heavens, and severed from the mercy of Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

"I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed." The servant invokes Allah—the proper Name signifying divine majesty—against Satan, whom Allah has taught us to regard as our enemy and whom He has commanded us to take as an enemy. To take an enemy as an adversary means to fortify oneself against him and to seek refuge from him. The servant possesses nothing but his Lord; he returns to Him, takes shelter with Him, and seeks His protection from the evil of this creature, Iblīs.

There was a student who repeatedly visited a scholar in Khurāsān until he had memorized four thousand words of wisdom from him. When the time came to bid farewell and return to his homeland, the scholar said to him: "I shall teach you something more excellent than all the wisdom you have acquired. Tell me, does Satan exist in your lands?" The student replied: "Yes." The scholar asked: "Does he tempt and whisper to you?" The student said: "Yes." The scholar then asked: "When the enemy of Allah whispers to you, what do you do?" The student answered: "We resist him." The scholar said: "And when he returns?" The student replied: "We resist him again." The scholar asked: "And if he persists?" The student said: "We resist him continually."

The scholar said to him: "You lack the power to resist him on your own. Allah says: 'Indeed, he sees you, he and his tribe, from where you do not see them' (Q. 7:27). But when the enemy of Allah whispers to you, be like a guest upon whom a dog of the household owner has suddenly lunged. The guest does not wrestle with the dog itself; rather, he cries out to the master of the house for protection. So too, when Iblīs whispers to you, take refuge in your Lord. He will suffice you against his evil. Say:
"I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed."[11]

"And I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed." Evil takes many forms: it may touch one's religion—whether through disbelief, heresy, transgression, grave sins, or lesser offenses—all of which are afflictions to one's faith. Evil may afflict the body: illness, chronic disease, weakness, or timidity. Evil may strike one's possessions: the death of children, the loss of wealth. Each of these is a calamity. When the servant seeks refuge in Allah, he intends thereby to seek refuge from all forms of evil—that which concerns his religion, that which concerns his body, and that which concerns his worldly possessions, which are blessings from Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

Some have said that the form of seeking refuge contradicts the station of the knowers (al-ʿārifūn), for those who know Allah do not fear any save Him, Blessed and Exalted, for they see none but Him. Yet this is, in truth, an adornment in relating to Allah, for He Himself has commanded it. The servant must recognize his lowliness, his poverty, and his utter helplessness before his Creator. If he were to govern something other than himself, he might display might; yet before his Creator, he is merely a wretched, weak, powerless creature. Even against the weak Iblīs, he seeks refuge in Allah, for he is incapable of repelling him on his own. It is said: "Fear Allah for the severity of His punishment; fear one who fears Allah, for his supplication; and fear one who fears not Allah, for he has no reverence and will not abstain from any transgression."[12] Thus, seeking refuge in Allah is a testimony to trust in Allah and a manifestation of the servant's poverty and humility before the Creator, that He might deliver him from this enemy. It does not contradict the knowledge of those who know, but rather is an etiquette observed in the presence of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. And for those whose spiritual station is such that they do not perceive Satan at all—such a one has no need of seeking refuge. Some of the gnostics say: "We are a people who know not Satan," and Allah says: "Over My servants you have no authority" (Q. 15:42).

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was asked about Satan's temptation during the prayer. He replied: "That is pure faith."[13] Indeed, the thief does not enter a house in which there is nothing worth stealing. The disbelievers and hypocrites do not experience the temptation of Satan, for Satan has already finished his work with them.

All who perceive temptation are truly believers. From the purity of their faith springs the experience of temptation. The enemy wages war only against those who oppose him. As for those who are in agreement with him, he has already finished with them and has no need to tempt them further. Such a one does not even need to seek refuge.

One day the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went forth to the mosque. He encountered Iblīs, who said to him: "What brings you to this mosque of mine?" The Prophet replied: "For you to answer me questions. Of all creation, who is most hateful to you?" Iblīs answered: "You." The Prophet asked: "Then who?" Iblīs said: "A youth raised in obedience to Allah, Blessed and Exalted." The Prophet then asked: "Why do you prevent my community from prayer in congregation?" Iblīs replied: "Because when they are engaged in prayer, I am bound and imprisoned; I cannot move for the duration of their prayer."

"Why do you prevent them from fasting?" Iblīs answered: "When Ramadan enters, I am shackled and bound; I am motionless throughout the month." "Why do you prevent them from jihād?" Satan replied: "I am cast into an even stronger bondage when they do not abandon jihād." "Why do you prevent my community from giving charity?" Iblīs said: "I am cast into a raging fever; I cannot prevent them from giving charity."[14]

The Prophet ﷺ seized Iblīs and bound him with a rope, tying him to one of the pillars of the mosque. He said: "I shall leave him bound until morning, so that all the people may gather and see him." But then the Prophet recalled the words of Solomon, upon him be peace: "Grant me a kingdom such as has not been given to anyone before me" (Q. 38:35). Out of reverence for Solomon and his supplication, the Prophet showed mercy and released Satan.[15]

"I seek refuge in Allah from Satan the accursed. (In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate.)" Much disagreement exists regarding the basmala (Bismillāh): whether it is a verse of Sūrat al-Fātiḥa, a verse opening every sūra, or a verse of the Qur'ān alone. Some have said it is part of a verse appearing in the Qur'ān: "Peace be upon you from Solomon, saying: In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate" (Q. 27:30)—thus it is neither a complete verse of the Qur'ān nor a verse of al-Fātiḥa, particularly not in other sūras.[16] Others, most notably al-Shāfiʿī, have held that it is a complete verse within al-Fātiḥa.

Still others say the basmala is not a verse of al-Fātiḥa but is recited at its opening. The strongest evidence that the basmala constitutes a verse of al-Fātiḥa and of every sūra is this: it has been found written in the Qur'ānic manuscripts in the form in which the Qur'ān is recorded. Whatever is not from the Qur'ān is not permitted to be written in this manner. Moreover, it appears written at the head of every sūra—this is the most compelling proof that it is a verse of al-Fātiḥa and a verse opening every sūra. It has been transmitted from the Messenger of Allah that he said: "I did not know the end of one sūra and the beginning of another except through the basmala."[17] At the head of each sūra, Gabriel would recite: "In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate," whereby the Prophet would know that a new sūra was commencing.

The strongest argument that the basmala is indeed a verse of every sūra is that it has been preserved in the written form of the Qur'ānic text. Whatever is not from the Qur'ān may not be inscribed in this manner. The basmala appears at the head of every sūra—this is the most powerful evidence. Moreover, it has been transmitted from the Messenger of Allah: "I did not distinguish the end of one sūra from the beginning of another save through the basmala."[17] When Gabriel revealed a new sūra to the Prophet, he would precede it with "In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate," thus the Prophet would recognize that a new sūra had begun.

The second argument in support of the basmala's status is this: the basmala is itself a beginning in Allah's name, Blessed and Exalted. Allah commanded the prophets before the Messenger to commence all their affairs with the invocation of Allah's name. Noah, upon him be peace, said: "In the name of Allah is its sailing and its anchoring" (Q. 11:41). Solomon, upon him be peace, said: "In the name of Allah is it. That you exalt not yourselves against me" (Q. 27:30). The Prophet ﷺ was commanded in the Qur'ān to follow the guidance of all the prophets: "So follow their guidance" (Q. 6:90). Therefore, it was obligatory upon him to begin with the basmala as they had done before him. This obligation binds the Prophet himself and extends necessarily to us, his followers. "Follow him" (Q. 7:158). The Prophet was obliged to follow those prophets who preceded him; we are equally obliged to follow him.[18] Thus, the basmala is obligatory upon the Prophet and obligatory upon us as his followers.

When asked about the basmala, the Messenger of Allah said: "It is a name among the names of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and between it and the Greatest Name (al-ism al-aʿẓam) is only what lies between the white of the eye and the black of it."[19] This hadīth indicates the basmala's profound sanctity and its proximity to the divine names of highest power.

The Qur'ān opens with the letter bā out of humility, lowliness, and poverty. It does not elevate itself like the letter alif. The name "Allah" is derived either from al-suww (elevation) or from al-simaṯ (marks, signs), for the name rises together with its bearer, or the name serves as a mark identifying its referent. The most correct view is that it derives from elevation.[20] Because of this etymology, the Ash'arī school and the Muʿtazilīs have differed regarding the divine names: are they proper names (aʿlām) or descriptive appellations (ʿalāmāt)? The Ash'arīs hold that Allah's names are proper designations, not mere descriptions. The Muʿtazilīs, by contrast, maintain that the divine names are merely appellations affixed to Allah, claiming that from eternity Allah was without a name—only after creating creatures did He become named by them. This view is rejected by the Ash'arīs,[21] who maintain instead that Allah's names, Blessed and Exalted, are eternal. Allah was never without His names and attributes from the beginning to the end.

The divine names comprise names of essence (asmāʾ al-dhāt), names of attributes (asmāʾ al-ṣifāt), and names of acts (asmāʾ al-afʿāl). All of these, in relation to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, are eternal and have no beginning, while in relation to other than Allah they are contingent.[22] A human being has a name conjoined with his existence, but he may acquire additional names—"master of the house," "master of the shirt," "master of the book," "scholar," "poet"—all of which come to him after his being. Allah, Blessed and Exalted, is not thus; rather, He is named by all His names from eternity and is adorned with all His attributes from eternity. This is the greatest hope of the gnostic regarding the Divine, for Allah has named Himself al-Raḥmān, al-Raḥīm, al-Karīm, al-Ghafūr, al-ʿAfu, al-Muʿtī. Before any other being existed to stand in need of these names, Allah possessed them eternally. When creation appeared and creatures came to need His mercy, His forgiveness, His generosity, their hope in Him is strengthened.

"In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate"—we recite [or: I recite] by the name of Allah, Blessed and Exalted. The human commences every action by invoking Allah's name. The governing verb is known but omitted. According to the Baṣran school, a verb is supplied; according to the Kūfan school, a noun is supplied. In any case, the object is elided, and each governing word supplies what suits its governance. We ourselves now recite; we recite by the name of Allah—the prepositional phrase "in the name of Allah" attaches to what follows. We, the community, recite in the name of Allah. If you are alone, I recite by the name of Allah. If you are eating, [I eat] by the name of Allah. If you are dressing, [I dress] by the name of Allah. If I drink, [I drink] by the name of Allah. If I ride, [I ride] by the name of Allah. The supplied word suits the action performed by the speaker. We recite by the name of Allah.

"Allah" is a proper name designating necessary being (wājib al-wujūd), who is independent of all else, while all else is dependent upon Him. Scholars have debated the etymology of "Allah." Some say it is a primitive proper name, not derived. It is reported that Sībawayh was seen in paradise after his death, and when asked how he entered paradise, he replied: "Through my affirmation that Allah is the most known of all knowns." Others say it derives from aliha (to worship), as if to say: the one worshipped, the deity. Still others derive it from aliha (to be bewildered), for human intellects are bewildered by His greatness, Blessed and Exalted.[23] The consensus view, and the one most firmly established, is that "Allah" is a primitive proper name, not a derivative word,[24] and none but Allah, Blessed and Exalted, is named by this name.

The Arabs understood "the deity" as the creator of the heavens and the earth. "And if you ask them, 'Who created the heavens and the earth?' they will surely say, 'Allah'" (Q. 43:9). They possessed this knowledge. Yet their disbelief arose from their claim: "This is nothing but a mortal like us" (Q. 23:24). As for Allah being the creator of the heavens and the earth, the sustainer who grants protection and cannot be harmed, who provides food and is not fed—all the disbelievers affirmed and believed this. Their disbelief concerned the Messenger ﷺ.

"The Merciful" (al-Raḥmān) is an intensive form derived from mercy (raḥma). Mercy is a softness of heart when one beholds the needy in distress; the heart pains at this sight, and one acts with kindness. Such suffering is impossible for Allah, Blessed and Exalted. Every attribute we have said is impossible for Allah has a beginning and an end; the beginning is impossible for Him, while the end is possible. Heart-softness or heart-suffering is impossible for Him, Blessed and Exalted, but the act of kindness, which is the end-point of mercy, is possible and indeed belongs to Him. "The Merciful" denotes one who bestows great blessings. "The Compassionate" (al-Raḥīm) denotes one who bestows subtle blessings. "The Merciful" is an intensive form; the name "Compassionate" alone would have sufficed, yet both appear because "Compassionate" too is an intensive form with specific significance. Allah shows mercy to all His servants in this world, believer and disbeliever alike.

"The Compassionate" is an intensive form of the attribute itself; a human may show compassion without compassion being his nature, but Allah is Compassionate—He is the Merciful, having released mercy upon all creatures. His very essence is mercy: "He has prescribed mercy upon Himself" (Q. 6:12). "The Compassionate" is an attribute of essence by which He is described from eternity, and He has also bestowed compassion. This is what strengthens our hope: He acts not from necessity but from His very nature, which is mercy itself. "He has prescribed mercy upon Himself." The Messenger of Allah said: "Allah created one hundred mercies. He withheld ninety-nine and sent down one into the world. By this single portion, all the mercy in creation operates, and by it creatures show compassion to one another—even the beast lifting her hoof gently over her young does so through this single portion. When the Day of Resurrection arrives, He will join this portion to the ninety-nine, making them complete, and will bestow them exclusively upon those of faith. Thus, none receives mercy save the faithful."[25]

"In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate"—this consists of nineteen letters. The keepers of the hellfire (al-zabānīya) are nineteen angels: "Over it are nineteen" (Q. 74:30). Whoever recites "In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate" once, every letter stands between him and one of these nineteen, and he shall never enter the fire.[26] Thus it is protection from hellfire's entry.

"In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate" has been discussed by scholars of every discipline. As for the people of the mysteries (ahl al-asrār), the hadīth suffices for them: "A name among the names of Allah, and between it and the Greatest Name is only what lies between the black of the eye and the white."[27] As for the grammarians, they have analyzed it syntactically, as has been mentioned: it is a phrase governed by an understood verb—the Baṣran grammarians supply a verbal element, the Kūfan grammarians a nominal element. In either case, it constitutes a minor clause.
Sūrat al-Fātiḥa
Meccan—seven verses.

This sūra is Meccan because the prayer obligation was revealed in Mecca, and the prayer has never been valid without Sūrat al-Fātiḥa.[29] It is, by consensus, a Meccan sūra. Some exegetes maintain it was revealed twice. It is Meccan, and it comprises seven verses.

Sūrat al-Fātiḥa is called by many names,[30] and the multiplicity of names indicates the nobility of the named. Among these are "the Opening of the Book" (Fātiḥat al-Kitāb)—meaning that with which the Book is opened, fātiḥa being derived from the root of ʿāfiya (well-being). It is called "the Mother of the Qur'ān" (Umm al-Qurʾān) and "the Mother of the Book" (Umm al-Kitāb), "the Seven Oft-Repeated Verses" (al-Sabʿ al-Mathānī), and "the Glorious Qur'ān." "We have surely given you seven of the oft-repeated verses and the Glorious Qur'ān" (Q. 15:87). It is called "the Treasure" (al-Kanz) because the Prophet said: "It was sent down to me as a treasure beneath the Throne."[32] It is called "the Sūra of Prayer" (Sūrat al-Ṣalāt) because prayer is not valid without it.

It is also called "the Prayer" itself (al-Ṣalāt). Sūrat al-Fātiḥa is called the Prayer, according to the hadīth: "The prayer is divided between Me and My servant in halves: half for Me and half for My servant, and My servant receives what he asks."[33] It is called "the Supplication" (al-Duʿāʾ) and "the Teaching of Supplication" (Taʿlīm al-Duʿāʾ). It is called "the Sufficiency" (al-Kāfiya) and "the Protection" (al-Wāqiya). It is called "the Healing Spell" (al-Ruqya) according to the hadīth: "What makes you know that it is a healing spell?"[34] It is also called "the One That Heals" (al-Rāqiya).

It is called "the Healing" (al-Shifāʾ) because it has been transmitted that Sūrat al-Fātiḥa is a cure for every ailment except death (al-sāmm).[35] Death (al-sāmm) means literally death itself. It is called "the Foundation" (al-Asās)[36] because it is the foundation of this religion called Islam.
It is called "the Light" (al-Nūr), "the Sūra of Praise" (Sūrat al-Ḥamd), and "the Sūra of Gratitude" (Sūrat al-Shukr). These are the names of this sūra, the most noble of all sūras in the Qur'ān.
The Messenger of Allah was asked: "Which of the Qur'ān is most excellent?" The people replied: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "Sūrat al-Fātiḥa."[37]

It is related that al-Ḥasan ibn ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face, fell severely ill. The Prophet ﷺ grieved for him. Gabriel descended, upon him be peace, and said: "Recite the sūra that contains no letter fāʾ over water to wash al-Ḥasan with it; by this he shall be cured of his illness." The Prophet searched and found that Sūrat al-Fātiḥa contained no letter fāʾ, because the letter fāʾ is a harbinger of separation (al-firāq).[38]

The Prophet recited the sūra over the water and washed al-Ḥasan with it. It was as though he had been freed from a bond. The Messenger of Allah said: "It is a healing from every ailment except death."

A group of the Prophet's companions traveled and stopped in a settlement of the Arabs. They asked for supper but were refused food in their miserliness. During the night, a serpent bit the settlement's chief. They came to the travelers and asked: "Is there anyone among you who knows how to heal?" One of them said: "Yes, I can heal, but you refused us supper. We shall not heal your chief unless you pay us." They asked: "How much?" He said: "A flock of sheep." They gave him a flock of sheep. He recited Sūrat al-Fātiḥa over the chief, the poison descended, and he was healed instantly.

The man said: "I shall take this flock to the Messenger of Allah to ask him whether it is lawful or unlawful." He came to the Prophet and informed him of what had transpired. The Messenger of Allah said: "And what makes you know that it is a healing spell? Divide the flock among your companions and take a share for me."[39] Thus he understood it was lawful. For this reason, this sūra is called "the Healing Spell" (al-Ruqya).

It has been transmitted from the Messenger of Allah that Allah sent down one hundred and four books: fifty upon Sheeth ibn Adam, upon him be peace; thirty upon Idrīs (Enoch); ten upon Abraham; and ten upon Moses before the Torah, as well as the Torah, the Psalms, the Gospels, and the Criterion.[40]

All these books were collected into the Four (the Torah, Psalms, Gospels, and Qur'ān). These Four were collected into the Criterion (the Qur'ān). And the entire Qur'ān is collected into Sūrat al-Fātiḥa. Thus, whoever recites Sūrat al-Fātiḥa has recited the entire Qur'ān, has recited the Four Books, and has recited all the heavenly scriptures.[41] It encompasses all the Qur'ān. The Qur'ān contains nine types of content:

The art of praise—you find in the Qur'ān verses praising Allah abundantly and extolling Him. The art of promise and warning. Within the Qur'ān you find both law (sharīʿa) and mystical truth (ḥaqīqa). Within it you find supplication, narrative accounts of those before us, admonition and remembrance, reports and tawhīd (testimony of divine unity). "All praise belongs to Allah"—this encompasses all that is due to Allah in praise and gratitude throughout the Qur'ān. Every eulogy and laudation of Allah is absorbed within "All praise belongs to Allah." "Lord of the worlds"—this is tawhīd. "The Merciful, the Compassionate"—this is promise. "Master of the Day of Judgment"—this is warning.

"You alone we worship"—this is law (sharīʿa). "You alone we call upon for aid"—this is mystical truth (ḥaqīqa). "Guide us to the Straight Path"—this is supplication. "The path of those upon whom You have bestowed Your grace"—this is narrative. "Not the path of those upon whom rests wrath, nor of those who go astray"—this is admonition and remembrance.
Thus all nine dimensions of the Qur'ān are contained within Sūrat al-Fātiḥa.[42]

Allah has mentioned five of His names in al-Fātiḥa, Blessed and Exalted: "All praise belongs to Allah," "Allah" (a name), "Lord of the worlds" (rabb is a name), "the Merciful" (a name), "the Compassionate" (a name), "Master of the Day of Judgment" (a name). These are the foundation of five principles. Islam is built upon five [pillars]: the testimony that there is no deity save Allah.[43] The meaning of "there is no deity save Allah" is: Allah. "And the establishment of prayer"—the Lord (rabb) means the one who nurtures and reforms; the servant's prayer nurtures and reforms his faith. "The Merciful"—this is fasting, an intensive form denoting mercy. The servant reaches such compassion for the needy that he tastes the hunger the poor endure, so that he may give charity to him. This is the pillar of fasting. "The Compassionate"—this is the pillar of alms (zakāt); he has compassion for the needy and removes a portion of his wealth for them. "Master of the Day of Judgment"—this is the pillar of pilgrimage, for just as people are gathered from all corners to the place of assembly, so do they gather for the Pilgrimage.

It is understood at the beginning of al-Fātiḥa that [we] say: "All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds." For the end of al-Fātiḥa proceeds from the servant's speech, if [we] do not supply "say," then al-Fātiḥa would appear to begin with the Lord's speech and end with the servant's speech. To ensure that all of it emanates from the servant, we supply "Say": "All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Merciful, the Compassionate, Master of the Day of Judgment... Guide us to the Straight Path." This entire utterance proceeds from the servant's speech, naturally.

"All praise"—praise is the eulogy of the good, whether his attribute or his act. Four kinds of praise exist: praise by the Lord for the Lord, praise by the Lord for the servant, praise by the servant for the Lord, and praise by the servant for a servant like himself. All of this is praise, whether of attribute or act, belonging to Allah.

"All praise belongs to Allah"—Paradise has eight levels, and "All praise belongs to Allah" comprises eight letters. Whoever says "All praise belongs to Allah" is worthy of the eight ranks of Paradise.[44] "Lord of the worlds"—Master of all creation. The worlds (ʿālamūn) is a collective plural, and the world is all that is other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted. It is pluralized in the masculine to encompass all created things. "The Merciful"—the Bestower of great and evident blessings. "The Compassionate"—the Bestower of subtle and hidden blessings. "Master of the Day of Judgment"—the Sovereign on the Day of Recompense. Sovereignty exists each day, but each day finds some rival to Allah's dominion in some part of the created realm. Yet on the Day of Resurrection, there is no rival to His dominion. Therefore He speaks: "To whom belongs dominion this Day?" (Q. 40:16). He receives no answer from any human, so He answers Himself: "To Allah, the One, the Irresistible" (Q. 40:16).

When the servant extolled his Lord by saying, "All praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds, the Merciful, the Compassionate, Master of the Day of Judgment," he thereby merited to be addressed. The divine presence addressed him, saying: "You alone we worship, and You alone we call upon for aid." None do we worship save You; none do we call upon save You. When the servant has praised his Lord, the divine presence grants him permission: "Ask of Me whatsoever you desire." The servant then says:

"Guide us to the Straight Path"—he petitions Allah, Blessed and Exalted, for guidance to the Straight Path. The Straight Path is the path of the Prophets and Messengers. "The path of those upon whom You have bestowed Your grace"—the Prophets. Upon some of them Allah bestowed grace: "Or are they envious of people for what Allah has given them of His bounty? We gave the family of Abraham the Book and wisdom, and We gave them a great kingdom" (Q. 4:54). Upon some of them Allah sent trial with the gravest afflictions. Had it said "the path of those whom You tried" or "the path of those who were slain" or "the path of those who were slaughtered," the servant would have feared. But in kindness to the servant, to encourage him, and to gladden his heart, it says "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed Your grace"—not all the Prophets receive grace; some are tried with the severest trials. "Among the Prophets and the truthful, the martyrs, and the righteous, and how excellent are those as companions!" (Q. 4:69).

"Not the path of those upon whom rests wrath"—it is related from the Messenger of Allah that these are the Jews, and the Qur'ān describes them as those upon whom wrath has descended. The Jews are those who possessed knowledge yet did not act upon it; therefore, wrath descended upon them. "Nor of those who go astray"—it is related from the Messenger of Allah that these are the Christians.[45] The Christians strayed from the way; they knew it not. They knew nothing—they were ignorant, so much so that in their profound ignorance they made a servant a lord. The Jews possessed knowledge but did not act upon it; the Christians were merely ignorant. "Not the path of those upon whom rests wrath, nor of those who go astray. 'Āmīn' is not from the Qur'ān; rather, it is the seal of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, like the seal with which a king stamps his correspondence."[46]
Sūrat Al-Baqara: The Cow
Sūrat al-Baqara comprises two hundred and eighty-six verses.

"In the name of Allah, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Alif. Lām. Mīm."[71] Allah knows best His intention. "That is the Book, in which there is no doubt" (Q. 2:2)—This Book which Muhammad ﷺ recites is without doubt sent down from Allah, Blessed and Exalted. There is no doubt regarding this. Even if Abū Jahl and his like expressed doubt, they are fools and madmen lacking intellect. Their doubt is as nothing; doubt itself renders void the doubting. The sun is the sun even if the blind perceive it not; honey is honey even if the sick taste it not. The Qur'ān is without doubt even if the foolish doubt it, for it came with overwhelming proofs and decisive arguments that it comes not from any save Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

"A guidance for those who fear [Allah]"—a guide for the wayfaring toward godwariness. This Book guides Allah thereby all whom He decreed in eternity to be journeying toward godwariness. "Those who believe in the unseen"—these are they who believed in what remained hidden from them. The unseen takes two forms: the unseen that lies hidden from you—the Paradise and the Hellfire, the angels, the houris, the resurrection and what lies beyond it. All of this lies hidden from you, yet you believed in it. And the unseen from which you yourself are hidden—this is the divine presence, Blessed and Exalted. You say it is hidden; rather, it is manifest, nearer to you than all else. If you do not find it, you yourself are the hidden one, not it. "Those who believe in the unseen." "And establish the prayer"—they perform the prayer in its completeness. "And from what We have provided for them, they spend"—they expend of what We have provided.

"And those who believe in what has been sent down to you"—which is the Qur'ān—"and what was sent down before you"—Faith in what was sent down before the Messenger does not benefit unless one believes in what was sent down to the Prophet ﷺ. Therefore, whoever believes in all the Prophets yet disbelieves in the Prophet of his time is a disbeliever. Similarly, whoever believes in all the saints yet disbelieves in the perfected one of his age is severed from Allah, Blessed and Exalted. Faith in what was sent down before you avails only when coupled with faith in what was sent down to you, and faith in what was sent down before you. "And in the Hereafter they have certainty"—they are certain of the Hereafter.

"Those are upon guidance from their Lord"—the guidance we requested in al-Fātiḥa, these who were described with these attributes found it. "And those—they are the successful"—the cutoff-assured regarding their victory, certain of their salvation from the Fire and their entry into eternal Paradise.

The sūra opens with four verses about believers, two verses about disbelievers, and thirteen verses about the hypocrites. Then it calls the servants to divine unity, belief in His Messenger, Paradise and the Hellfire. Then it addresses the Children of Israel in half the sūra. Then it presents the jurisprudence of the religion: "Prescribed for you in retaliation is life" (Q. 2:178). The four attributes at the beginning of the sūra correspond to the four Rightly-Guided Caliphs. First mentioned is "a guidance for those who fear [Allah]"—godwariness (taqwā) is the attribute of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him. "And those saved from it is the one who spends in charity to purify himself" (Q. 92:18)—this verse was revealed regarding Abū Bakr by agreement.

Faith in the unseen is the attribute of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, may Allah be pleased with him. When ʿUmar embraced Islam, Gabriel descended upon the Messenger saying: "The Messenger has sufficiency in Allah and in those believers who follow him" (Q. 8:64). Faith is ʿUmar's attribute. "And establish the prayer"—this is the attribute of ʿUthmān, may Allah be pleased with him. "Is one who is devoutly obedient during the night hours, prostrating and standing" (Q. 39:9)—this verse was revealed regarding ʿUthmān. He would stand through the night with the Qur'ān.

"And from what We have provided for them, they spend"—this is the attribute of ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib, may Allah honor his face. He hired himself out in a Jewish orchard and worked until he earned four dirhams. He gave one in charity publicly, one in secret, one by night, and one by day.[47] Expenditure is the attribute of ʿAlī, may Allah honor his face. All who are adorned with these attributes stand beneath the banners of these four on the Day of Resurrection. Expenditure increases the servant's wealth and does not diminish it.[48] "Every sunrise comes with two angels at its side, one saying: 'O Allah, grant the spender a worthy replacement,' while the other says: 'O Allah, bring loss to the hoarder.'"[49]

It is related that a servant of Allah asked a Prophet to beseech Allah to grant him wide provision. The Prophet prayed to Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and Allah answered his prayer. Allah said: "Inform My servant that I have divided his lifespan into two halves: one half poverty, one half wealth. Let him choose which shall come first." That Prophet called the man and informed him. The man consulted his wife. She said: "Tell him that the wide provision should come to you now."

The man said to her: "Poverty after wealth is exceedingly difficult." She said: "Do not disobey me; seek wealth now only." He came to that Prophet and said: "Let the wealth come to me now." The wealth came to him. His wife said to him: "If you stitch a garment for yourself, give a garment in charity to the poor. If you buy food for yourself, buy the like of it in charity to the poor. If you build a house, build one like it for the poor. If you buy a mount, do likewise for the poor. Whatever you do for yourself, do the like of it for the destitute." He acted thus, and what he had increased until half his lifespan had passed. Then Allah revealed to the Prophet: "I had decreed his lifespan half poverty and half wealth, but I found him grateful. So I decreed his entire lifespan wealth; he shall never know poverty."[50]

Thus expenditure diminishes not the provision. The Messenger of Allah said: "Upon every joint of the child of Adam there is due a charity each day."[51] The human comprises joints numbering the days of the year—three hundred and sixty-five parts. For each part, you must bestow a charity each day. The people asked: "O Messenger of Allah, who is capable of this?" He replied: "Commanding good is charity, two units of prayer is charity, assisting your brother in his need—whether accomplished or not—is charity, and gladdening hearts with all kindnesses. Allah perfects these charities with them."
O Allah, bless our master Muhammad and grant him peace.

O Allah, bless our master Muhammad, the opener of what was closed, the sealer of what preceded, the helper of the truth through truth, and the guide to Your Straight Path. We ask Allah, Blessed and Exalted, to grant us and you understanding of this Book and to act upon it, and to perfect for us this action just as He began it for us, through the intercession of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Write us in the register of the fortunate in this world and the next. O Allah, bless our master Muhammad and grant him peace.
O Allah, bless our master Muhammad and grant him peace.

"I seek refuge in Allāh from Satan the accursed. By Allāh's Name, The Entirely Merciful, The Especially Merciful."

O Allah, bestow blessings upon our master Muḥammad, the opener of what had been closed and the seal of what had preceded, the helper of truth through truth, the guide to Your straight path, and upon his family, the true measure of his worth and his immense station. May Allah be pleased with the Companions of the Messenger of Allah, ṣ.a.w.s.

Having described the elect among His slaves with those qualities and mentioned their ultimate destination, He followed this with the description of His enemies. He dedicated four verses to the characteristics of the believers, two verses to the disbelievers, and thirteen verses to the hypocrites.

Kufr (disbelief) linguistically means covering and concealing. In the terminology of Islamic law, it signifies the denial of something whose arrival from the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., is necessarily known. Al-kāfir (the disbeliever) appears in the Qurʾān in four categories: (1) the disbeliever as the opposite of the believer, as in "Verily those who disbelieve and hinder from the path of Allah" (Q. 4:167); (2) the disbeliever in the sense of one who denies, as in "whoever rejects it — Allah is Self-Sufficient, above all the worlds" (Q. 3:97), meaning whoever denies the obligation of ḥajj; (3) the disbeliever as the opposite of the grateful, as in "Give thanks to Me and do not disbelieve" (Q. 2:152); and (4) the disbeliever in the sense of one who disavows, as in "then on the Day of Resurrection you will disavow one another and curse one another" (Q. 29:25), meaning you will disavow one another.[1]

The varieties of kufr are as follows. The kufr of the knowing denier: one who knows the existence of the True, Blessed and Exalted, and yet denies Him by tongue, as in the kufr of Iblīs and the kufr of the Jews: "and when there came to them that which they recognized, they disbelieved in it" (Q. 2:89). The kufr of absolute negation: denying the existence of the Creator entirely, as with most disbelievers. The kufr of one who knows the truth inwardly but does not profess it by tongue and does not practice the religion, as occurred with Abū Ṭālib, who said in verse: "Verily I know that the religion of Muḥammad / is among the best of all the religions of mankind." He uttered this with his tongue and believed it in his heart, yet he did not enter Islām and thus died a disbeliever. And the kufr of hypocrisy (al-nifāq): professing belief by tongue while denying it in the heart.

Kufr, as we established, is the denial of something whose arrival from the Prophet Muḥammad, ṣ.a.w.s., is necessarily known: the oneness of Allah, Blessed and Exalted; the performance of prayers; fasting Ramaḍān; the obligatory nature of zakāh on wealth; ḥajj; and the Resurrection. Whatever is necessarily known to have come from the Prophet, its denial is kufr. As for what cannot be known to have come from the Prophet except through careful investigation and discernment, one who denies it does not become a disbeliever. The distinguishing marks which the scholars have enumerated as acts of kufr — such as wearing the zunnār (the monk's belt) and the ghiyār — are signs of kufr, not kufr in themselves. Whoever is seen wearing the zunnār is declared with certainty to be no believer, because the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., forbade it; yet it carries no self-gratification the way fornication or wine-drinking do. Those are forbidden by the Law, but they contain pleasure for the lower self, and whoever commits them is not a disbeliever because the self overcame him through desire. But wearing the zunnār carries no pleasure whatsoever: whoever wears it has contemptuously dismissed the Islamic religion, and he is a disbeliever. Anyone who meets Allah, Blessed and Exalted, bearing any form of kufr will dwell forever in the Fire: "Verily Allah does not forgive that anything be associated with Him, and He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills" (Q. 4:48).

(Verily those who disbelieve) — that is, people such as Abū Jahl, Abū Lahab, and those like them among the disbelievers — (it is equal to them whether you warn them or you do not warn them: they will not believe), because Allah, Blessed and Exalted, knew this of them; so do not aspire to their faith.

The True, Blessed and Exalted, informed His Prophet that these disbelievers would never believe. He did not say "it is equal to you whether you warn them or not," for warning and leaving warning are not equal concerning the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., since he is obligated to convey the message. If he conveys it, whether anyone believes or not, he is rewarded. But as for the disbelievers who will not believe: warning and not warning them are equal to them, for they will never believe. Allah informed His Prophet of this in advance so as to cut off his hope for their faith, so that he might not suffer as Nūḥ suffered. After spending one thousand minus fifty years among his people, Allah revealed to him: "None of your people will believe except those who have already believed" (Q. 11:36). After enduring those tribulations, Allah informed him. But the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., was told in advance, so that he would not long for their faith. And when Nūḥ came to know that his people would not believe, he called down destruction upon them; but the Prophet, upon learning that his people would not believe, did not call down destruction upon them, for he is the Prophet of Mercy: "We did not send you save as a mercy to all the worlds" (Q. 21:107).

Allah, Blessed and Exalted, established in this verse that warning them and not warning them are equal. The disbelievers themselves acknowledged this regarding their prophet Hūd: "It is equal to us whether you admonish us or are not among those who admonish" (Q. 26:136). And in the hereafter, when they are cast into the Fire, they will be told: "Bear it patiently or do not — it is the same for you" (Q. 52:16). Just as Allah declared it equal for them in this world regarding warning, so they are made to know in the Fire that their patience and their impatience are alike. And they themselves say: "Whether we are distressed or patient, it is the same for us: there is no way out for us" (Q. 14:21).

(Allah has set a seal on their hearts), stamped upon them and locked them so that no good enters them, (and on their hearing), so they are unable to benefit from the truth they hear, (and on their eyes is a covering), so they cannot see the truth. (And for them is a mighty punishment): a powerful and eternal chastisement, which is the Fire. "Mighty" (ʿaẓīm) is the opposite of paltry, just as "great" (kabīr) is the opposite of small, and ʿaẓīm surpasses kabīr in degree. This punishment is exceedingly severe, severer than every other punishment. This concerns the disbelievers.

And this was revealed concerning the hypocrites, such as ʿAbdullāh ibn Ubayy ibn Salūl and his companions, who when they came to the Muslims said to them "We are with you," and when they went to the disbelievers said "We are with you."

(And among the people are those who say: "We believe in Allah and in the Last Day"), that is, the Day of Resurrection, called "the Last Day" because it is the final of all days, (yet they are not believers). The plural form is used in accordance with the sense of "those among the people." (They seek to deceive Allah and those who believe), by displaying outwardly the opposite of what they conceal inwardly of disbelief, so as to ward off from themselves the worldly consequences of kufr. (Yet they deceive none but themselves): because the harm of their deception returns to them. They are exposed in this world through Allah's informing His Prophet of what they concealed, and they will be punished in the hereafter. (And they do not perceive it.)

As for the grammatical note: yukhādiʿūna here is a form of the pattern fāʿala, which normally denotes mutuality between two parties, but here it applies to one party alone, just as one might say in Arabic "I punished the thief" or "I treated the patient," using fāʿala without a partner. The mention of Allah in "they seek to deceive Allah" is an elevation of the Muslims' station, for in truth they are only deceiving the believers; but Allah made the deception of the Muslims equivalent to deceiving Him, Blessed and Exalted.

(In their hearts is a disease), that is, doubt and hypocrisy, which ail their hearts. (So Allah increased their disease) through what He sent down of the Qurʾān, because they rejected it. This disease may be understood as spiritual: the doubt and hypocrisy in their hearts is a moral sickness. Or it may be understood as a genuine physical pain, because the continuous and ever-increasing strength of the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., and the growing might of the Muslims caused them anguish until it became as though a bodily disease. (And for them is a painful punishment), a torment that causes pain, (because they used to lie) — in the reading of Ḥafṣ — or "because they used to disbelieve" in the reading of Warsh.[2]
<div class="en-footnotes">

[2] The reading kadhhabū ('they used to lie') is that of the majority transmission, including the reading of Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim. The variant kafarū ('they used to disbelieve') is the reading transmitted via Warsh from Nāfiʿ, which is the primary reading of North and West Africa. Both readings are canonical (mutawātir) and carry independent exegetical weight; the Warsh variant sharpens the alignment of the verse with the preceding descriptions of unbelief.

(And when it is said to them), these hypocrites, ("Do not spread corruption in the earth"), through disbelief and diverting people from faith, (they say: "We are only reformers"), claiming that what they do is not corruption but rather merely maintaining relations with both sides and serving their own interests. But in truth they are only corrupters. Allah declared: (Unquestionably, it is they who are the corrupters — but they do not perceive it). Alā is a particle of alertness. "Innahum hum al-mufsidūn" carries double emphasis. But the triple emphasis with the lām of affirmation is absent, because they do not actively perceive their own corruption; they genuinely believe themselves to be reformers.

A philosopher once posed a question to a scholar: "We see redundancy in Arabic speech — people say 'Zayd is standing,' then 'Indeed Zayd is standing,' then 'Indeed Zayd is certainly standing.' Is this not mere padding?" The Arab scholar replied: "'Zayd is standing' is a straightforward declaration of Zayd's standing. 'Indeed Zayd is standing' is an answer to an implied question. 'Indeed Zayd is certainly standing' is a refutation of someone who denies it." The hypocrites said "We believe" using a verbal form (āmannā), a lighter and less committed expression. Allah replied to them: "They are not believers," using the nominal form with the negation of mā, which is stronger, for it expels them entirely from the totality of believers. Had He said only "they did not believe," that alone would not have removed them from the community of believers.

(And when they meet those who believe, they say: "We believe"), using the verbal form: lighter in expression. But when they returned (to their satans), their chiefs and leaders, (they say: "We are with you"), using the nominal form with inna, a stronger assertion of loyalty. ("We were only mocking") them by displaying belief. (Allah mocks them), requiting them for their mockery. (And He extends them in their transgression), giving them respite in their exceeding of all bounds through kufr, (wandering blindly). (Those are they who purchased error in exchange for guidance): they took misguidance in place of guidance. (So their trade brought no profit, and they were not guided) in what they did.

Then Allah struck two parables for the hypocrites, for a parable affords the clearest possible illustration: it represents what is absent through what is present, and what is conceptual through what is sensory. (Their likeness), their condition in their hypocrisy, (is as the likeness of one who kindled a fire), one who lit a fire in darkness. (When it illumined all around him), when he could see and had found warmth and protection from what he feared, (Allah took away their light), extinguishing it. He did not say "took away their fire" because the purpose in kindling a fire is the light it produces. (And He left them in darknesses unable to see), confused and confounded about the way, fearful. Just so, these hypocrites believed by uttering the word of faith; when they die, fear and punishment come upon them. (Deaf): they are deaf to the truth and do not hear it with a hearing of acceptance. (Dumb): mute in goodness and unable to utter it. (Blind): to the path of guidance and unable to see it. (They will not return) from misguidance.

(Or like a rainstorm from the sky), or their likeness is as those beneath a rain shower, (in which are darknesses): the darkness of night, the darkness of heavy cloud, and the darkness of falling rain. (And thunder), the angel charged with the rain, or its sound. (And lightning), its flash. (They put their fingers into their ears against the thunderbolts, fearing death) from hearing it. Just so, these hypocrites: when the Qurʾān descended containing the mention of kufr, likened to darkness, and threats against it, likened to thunder, and its clear proofs, likened to lightning, they stopped their ears so as not to hear it, lest they be moved to believe in what they heard that they desired, and lest they be held to what they loathed. This is the parable of the hypocrites.[3]

The hypocrite is a disbeliever at heart; yet seeing the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., bearing a sword, killing those who opposed him and seizing their wealth, he came and pronounced the two testimonies of faith: "There is no god but Allah; Muḥammad is the Messenger of Allah," though he was not sincere in his heart. He prayed with the Muslims and gave charity. By this he protected himself and his wealth in life. But death is inevitable; and when he dies, he enters a punishment far more severe than what he had feared in life.

(Had Allah willed, He would have taken away their hearing), meaning their ears, (and their sight. Verily Allah is over all things powerful), including the taking of what has been mentioned.

The Qurʾān has now established the descriptions of the believers, the disbelievers, and the hypocrites. The Qurʾān began with the "clear" (muḥkam), Sūrat al-Fātiḥa, a perfectly composed sūra, and followed with Sūrat al-Baqara, the first verse of which is "ambiguous" (mutashābih): "Alif. Lām. Mīm." These letters are the weightiest thing for the Arabs, because they understood nothing of what these letters contain. The Qurʾān, in its miraculous nature, is recognized through its eloquence, its rhetorical excellence, and its knowledge of the unseen. The Arabs understood everything that appeared in the Qurʾān until these letters appeared at the openings of certain sūras, and they could discern not the faintest trace of their meaning. These letters are the hardest thing upon them.

Every Arabic word drawn from the roots of the language carries a meaning that matches the nature of the root. For example, the root k-l-m carries in the Arabic language the meaning of force and intensity. This meaning appears in all its derivations: the kalima (word) is so called because it strikes the hearing and the mind of a person until he grasps its meaning; kalam in another sense is the grievous wound, a severe strike. Every word of the Arabs has a derivation and variations. The kalima appears in the Qurʾān in the sense of ʿĪsā, who is called "a word" because he came into being from the command "kun" (Be!), without the agency of a father. And in the usage of the Arabs, they call a full ode a kalima and a sermon a kalima. The Messenger, ṣ.a.w.s., said: "The truest word the poet ever uttered is the word of Labīd: 'Truly, everything besides Allah is vanishing.'" Yet these disconnected letters: the Arabs found in them no trace of meaning. They are therefore the greatest miracle for the Arabs, surpassing all the other miracles of the Qurʾān.[4][5]

When the first of the disconnected letters, "Kāf. Hā. Yā. ʿAyn. Ṣād.," was revealed, Jibrīl would normally recite the whole verse to the end and then explain it, and the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., would repeat it as Jibrīl had recited it and explain it as well. But when Jibrīl brought the revelation "Kāf," the Prophet said: "I understand." "Hāʾ" — "I understand." "Yāʾ" — "I understand." "ʿAyn" — "I understand." "Ṣād" — "I understand." The Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., knew their meanings before Jibrīl knew them. Jibrīl thereby came to know that this is a secret concealed even from him, the very one charged with conveying the revelation.[6]

They explain that he is called 'a word from Him' because he came into existence through the divine command kun (Be!), without the agency of a father, unlike all other created beings. Ibn Kathīr transmits the same explanation in his commentary on Q. 3:39.

[5] Al-Bukhārī transmits in his Ṣaḥīḥ (no. 6147) from Abū Hurayra that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, said: 'The truest word the poet ever uttered is the word of Labīd: Alā kull shayʾin mā khalā llāha bāṭilu — Truly, everything besides Allah is vanishing.' Muslim transmits the same hadith (no. 4187). Labīd ibn Rabīʿa al-ʿĀmirī was a celebrated pre-Islamic poet who subsequently embraced Islām and ceased composing poetry.

[6] The tradition of Jibrīl pausing at each disconnected letter while the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, responded 'I understand' (fahimtu) at each one, establishing that the Prophet possessed foreknowledge of their meaning before the angel himself had disclosed it, is cited by al-Bursawī in Rūḥ al-Bayān, vol. 28, p. 166, in the context of the opening letters of Sūrat Maryam (Kāf. Hā. Yāʾ. ʿAyn. Ṣād.). The tradition underscores the distinction between prophetic knowledge (ʿilm ladunnī) and angelic knowledge of transmitted revelation.

The Sheikh, r.a., describes the believers and adorns them with the finest qualities: taqwā (God-consciousness), faith in the unseen (al-ghayb), the establishment of prayer (iqāmat al-ṣalāh), and spending from what Allah has provided them.

Prayer is mentioned by Allah in the Qurʾān in a number of verses: "Establish the prayer" (aqīmū al-ṣalāh), meaning not merely to perform a prayer but to establish it, to erect it and perfect it and correct it in every aspect so that it contains no deficiency. Allah commanded the performance of prayer in congregation: "and bow with those who bow" (Q. 2:43). And He commanded that it be performed with full inward submission: "those who are humble in their prayers" (Q. 23:2).

The Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., and those who followed him, may Allah make us and you among them, fulfilled all of these commands entirely: they established the prayer, performed it in congregation and in its proper time, and humbled themselves within it. Allah mentioned them and mentioned their final destination: "Those are the inheritors who shall inherit al-Firdaws; therein they shall abide" (Q. 23:10-11).

He also mentioned those who stand in contrast: those who "belied and turned away" (Q. 75:32) and their recompense: "What has brought you into Saqar? They said: 'We were not among those who prayed'" (Q. 74:42-43). And those who came after and neglected prayer: "Then there followed after them a generation who wasted the prayer and followed desires; they shall encounter perdition" (Q. 19:59). Whenever Allah mentions prayer, He joins it with zakāh, because prayer is the greatest act of bodily worship and spending in charity is the greatest act of worship with wealth; and no one's religion is complete unless he worships with both his body and his wealth.
Having described the disbelievers, the hypocrites, and the believers, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, then called all of humanity to His oneness, which is the greatest of all things.

(O Mankind), the people of Mecca and all who surround them from throughout the world, (worship), that is, unify, (your Lord who created you), who brought you into existence when you were nothing, (and those before you), and who created those before you, (so that perhaps you might be God-conscious): laʿalla in the speech of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, carries the force of certainty and confirmation. But from the perspective of the slave: Allah commands him to worship and to unify his Lord, yet the slave must not feel safe but must rather hope and fear. Thus "perhaps you might be God-conscious" requires no reinterpretation; the slave hopes to be among the muttaqīn and fears that he may not attain it.

He then explains the rationale for singling out Allah alone for worship: (He who made the earth a resting place for you), a spread-out expanse upon which to recline, not so hard that nothing can find rest upon it nor so soft that nothing can stand upon it. Allah made it firm yet yielding so that you may settle upon it standing, seated, or lying down. (And the sky a canopy): He who raised this roof above us. (And sent down from the sky water): the rain descends first from the sky, then reaches the clouds, then descends from the clouds to the earth. (By it He brought forth all kinds of fruits as provision for you), which you eat and with which you feed your animals. (So do not set up rivals to Allah), partners in worship, (while you know): do not worship other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted, while you know that He alone is the Creator. If a person knows that Allah is the Creator, he knows that none deserves his worship except Allah.

Among those of the deluded: one who knows that Allah created him yet does not worship Him; one who knows that Allah provides for him yet does not rely upon Him; one who knows this world passes away yet clings to it; one who knows his heirs will be his adversaries yet gathers wealth for them; one who knows death is coming yet has not prepared for it; one who knows with certainty the grave is his dwelling yet has not prepared it; one who knows with certainty the Bridge (al-ṣirāṭ) is his crossing yet has not lightened his load; one who knows with certainty the Fire is the abode of the wicked yet has not fled from it; one who knows with certainty Paradise is the dwelling of the beloved of Allah yet does not seek it; and one who knows with certainty that Iblīs is his enemy yet does not do battle with him.[7]

The categories of shirk (associating partners with Allah) are three: the manifest shirk, that practiced by the polytheists in the worship of idols; the hidden shirk, acting for the sake of reputation and public praise; and the most hidden shirk, perceiving anything other than Allah, Blessed and Exalted.

It is narrated that Allah has charged seven angels with the deeds of the slave. If he performs an act, the angels carry it upward; the angel of the lowest heaven examines it and says: "Return this deed upon its owner — he is a slanderer" or "a backbiter." In each successive heaven, deeds of arrogance, self-admiration, jealousy, ostentation, and love of fame are similarly returned. If a deed passes through all the heavens, Allah, Blessed and Exalted, says: "This person concealed from you what lies within him; but nothing is concealed from Me. This deed was not intended for My face — return it upon its owner, for he intended other than Me." For this reason it is narrated from the Messenger, ṣ.a.w.s.: "People are destroyed save the believers; the believers are destroyed save the scholars; the scholars are destroyed save those who act; those who act are destroyed save the sincere; and the sincere are in a state of peril."[8]
<div class="en-footnotes">

[7] The enumeration of 'ten of the deluded' (ʿasharat al-maghbūnīn) is a well-known didactic tradition in Sufi and ethical literature. Al-Ṣāwī cites a version of it in his Ḥāshiyat al-Ṣāwī ʿalā Tafsīr al-Jalālayn in the context of Q. 2:22, as an elaboration on the verse's call to worship Allah alone. The tradition appears in various forms across the classical literature of akhlāq and waʿẓ (homiletics), attributed to different early authorities.

[8] The tradition of the seven angels charged with the servant's deeds, each in successive heavens examining and returning deeds tainted by slander, backbiting, arrogance, self-admiration, jealousy, ostentation, and love of fame, is widely circulated in the literature of tazkiyat al-nafs (spiritual purification). The report concludes with Allah's refusal even of a deed that passed through all seven heavens but was not sincerely intended for His face alone. The tradition is cited in various forms by al-Ghazālī in Iḥyāʾ ʿUlūm al-Dīn and by later commentators on sincerity (ikhlāṣ).

(And if you are in doubt about what We sent down to Our slave), that is, the Prophet Muḥammad, ṣ.a.w.s., as to whether it is truly from Allah, (then bring a sūra like it): meet the challenge of the Qurʾān. Bring one sūra comparable to it in eloquence, beauty of composition, and knowledge of the unseen. The shortest sūra is Sūrat al-Kawthar, comprising three verses. (And call your witnesses), your gods whom you worship, (besides Allah, if you are truthful) in claiming that Muḥammad composed it himself. If you can do so, then do — for you are Arabs, eloquent and fluent like him.

The Qurʾān first challenged with the whole Qurʾān itself: "Say: if all of mankind and the jinn were to gather to produce the like of this Qurʾān, they could not produce the like of it, even if they were to one another supporters" (Q. 17:88). Then it challenged them with ten sūras: "Then bring ten invented sūras like it" (Q. 11:13). Then it challenged them with a single sūra, even the size of "We have surely given you al-Kawthar" — and they were unable. The Arabs, with all their eloquence and rhetorical mastery, did not come forward to compete with the Prophet, ṣ.a.w.s., in producing the like of the Qurʾān. The only one who dared was Musaylama the Arch-Liar, and Allah so disfigured his attempt that his words sounded as though they were not those of an Arab at all. His imitation of Sūrat al-Kawthar was: "We have given you jewels; pray to your Lord and make yourself manifest." What connection is there between jewels and prayer? Jewels are something of the adornments of this world, far removed from "We have surely given you al-Kawthar; so pray to your Lord and sacrifice."[9]

The Americans once commissioned a man learned in Arabic to compose something like Sūrat al-Fātiḥa. He said: "In the name of the Lord of all existence," abandoning the name Allāh, which is indispensable in speaking of Allah, Blessed and Exalted, and saying instead "Lord of all existence" (rabb al-akwān), abandoning "all the worlds" (al-ʿālamīn) for a modern coinage not found in classical Arabic. He then said "Yours is the worship and in You I seek help," intending to condense "You alone we worship and from You alone we seek help" (iyyāka naʿbudu wa-iyyāka nastaʿīn) into four words; but he turned al-mustaʿān into a verbal noun, distorting the grammar entirely. Anyone who hears these words knows immediately that they are not the speech of a native Arab, that the speaker has never mastered classical Arabic.
<div class="en-footnotes">

[9] Musaylama ibn Ḥabīb al-Ḥanafī, known as 'the Arch-Liar' (al-Kadhdhāb), was a claimant to prophethood in the Arabian Peninsula during and after the lifetime of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. His attempt to imitate Sūrat al-Kawthar, widely quoted by Muslim scholars as evidence of the Qurʾān's inimitability (iʿjāz), is cited in various tafsīr works including Ibn Kathīr's commentary and al-Suyūṭī's al-Itqān, chapter on the taḥaddī. He was killed at the Battle of Yamāma (12 AH / 633 CE) during the Ridda Wars.

(But if you do not do it — and you will never do it), if you are unable to produce what was asked of you, because you are incapable, and you never will be, (then fear) Allah through faith. (The Fire whose fuel is people), the disbelievers, (and stones), their idols which they had worshipped, (prepared for the disbelievers): it has been made ready for them; they will all be punished therein together.

(And give glad tidings to those who believe), who have affirmed faith in Allah, (and do righteous deeds), from the obligatory acts and the supererogatory acts, (that for them are gardens), orchards with trees and dwellings, (beneath which rivers flow): beneath their trees and their palaces flow the waters. The waters pour forth in Paradise without limit and without machinery; they flow with the inhabitants wherever they are needed.

(Every time they are given provision from its fruits, they say: "This is what we were given before" — and they are brought resemblance thereof): they are offered provision from the fruits of Paradise and say that this resembles what they received before. (And for them therein are purified spouses), purified from menstruation and from every impurity. (And therein they shall abide), dwelling there forever, neither dying nor ever departing from it.[10]

O Allah, bestow blessings upon our master Muḥammad, the opener of what had been closed and the seal of what had preceded, the helper of truth through truth, the guide to Your straight path, and upon his family, the true measure of his worth and his immense station.

See also the relevant discussions in Ibn Kathīr's commentary on Q. 44:54 and Q. 56:22-23.
